embedding_input:
Capability: Explain every chart and state its takeaway
Triggers: adding charts to slides; presenting trends or comparisons; writing slide titles
Method: 1. Include only charts that show a supported trend, relationship, comparison, or composition. 2. Explain what the audience is seeing and why it matters. 3. Write the supported takeaway in the title or presenter notes and reveal complexity only when relevant.
Constraints: Remove a chart when it has no clear explanatory role.
Citation: cdv-explain-every-chart | pages 182, 183 | references/storytelling.md#cdv-explain-every-chart

Capability: Critique a visualization against explicit standards
Triggers: reviewing an existing chart; prioritizing revisions; teaching visualization judgment
Method: 1. State the chart's intended audience, question, and takeaway. 2. Evaluate evidence, encoding, hierarchy, legibility, attribution, and unnecessary elements against the checklist. 3. Prioritize revisions by risk to interpretation before cosmetic polish.
Constraints: Tie every critique to observable evidence rather than taste alone.
Citation: cdv-critique-against-standards | pages 138, 163 | references/visual-design.md#cdv-critique-against-standards

Capability: Make the insight familiar and easy to spot
Triggers: an insight is hidden; a chart needs lengthy explanation; choosing an encoding
Method: 1. Name the trend, relationship, or comparison the audience must see. 2. Choose a familiar chart form that maps that relationship directly. 3. Reduce density and competing marks until the supported pattern is immediately discoverable.
Constraints: Do not simplify away uncertainty or material exceptions.
Citation: cdv-make-insight-familiar-and-obvious | pages 263 | references/data-visualization.md#cdv-make-insight-familiar-and-obvious

Capability: Separate exploratory analysis from explanatory communication
Triggers: finding patterns; moving from analysis to presentation; building a visualization workflow
Method: 1. Interrogate and visualize the data to discover patterns and candidate insights. 2. Test whether the insight survives analytical scrutiny. 3. Redesign the final display around the supported insight and audience decision.
Constraints: Do not publish an exploratory view as if it were a finished explanation.
Citation: cdv-explore-then-explain | pages 10, 27, 32, 85 | references/data-analysis.md#cdv-explore-then-explain

Capability: Contextualize scale for a diverse audience
Triggers: communicating percentages; small subsets; audiences unfamiliar with system size
Method: 1. Identify which denominator or system scale the audience may not know. 2. Pair rates or subsets with a truthful reference quantity or comparison. 3. Explain how the context changes interpretation without overwhelming the main finding.
Constraints: Use context that is comparable and decision-relevant.
Citation: cdv-contextualize-scale | pages 231 | references/data-visualization.md#cdv-contextualize-scale

Capability: Pair the insight with an appropriate display and attention cue
Triggers: highlighting a finding; comparing chart alternatives; directing attention
Method: 1. Write the insight before choosing the final display. 2. Compare candidate chart forms against the relationship the insight depends on. 3. Use one preattentive cue to direct attention to the decisive evidence.
Constraints: Do not highlight multiple competing focal points.
Citation: cdv-pair-insight-display-and-attention | pages 159 | references/data-visualization.md#cdv-pair-insight-display-and-attention

Capability: Guide the audience through a chart
Triggers: presenting a chart; explaining findings; designing for client questions
Method: 1. Start from what the audience already knows, does not know, and is trying to decide. 2. Introduce the chart context before asking viewers to interpret marks. 3. Direct attention progressively to the decisive points and reinforce the message with suitable narration.
Constraints: Never show a chart without context or an explanation of why it matters.
Citation: cdv-guide-audience-through-chart | pages 16, 136, 142, 148 | references/storytelling.md#cdv-guide-audience-through-chart

Capability: Match chart complexity to audience visual literacy
Triggers: choosing between familiar and novel charts; communicating to mixed-experience audiences
Method: 1. Estimate which chart forms and conventions the audience already understands. 2. Prefer a familiar encoding when it communicates the same finding clearly. 3. When a novel form is necessary, teach the reading pattern before presenting the conclusion.
Constraints: Do not make novelty a comprehension tax.
Citation: cdv-match-chart-to-visual-literacy | pages 156 | references/storytelling.md#cdv-match-chart-to-visual-literacy

Capability: Audit whether visuals form a coherent presentation
Triggers: reviewing a deck; checking chart sequence; planning post-presentation sharing
Method: 1. Check that the story is relevant to the topic and audience. 2. Verify each chart type and design choice supports its local takeaway. 3. Read the visuals in sequence and remove gaps, contradictions, or redundant evidence.
Constraints: Plan how shared slides will remain understandable without the live narration.
Citation: cdv-audit-presentation-coherence | pages 183, 185 | references/storytelling.md#cdv-audit-presentation-coherence

Capability: Select static, animated, or interactive presentation deliberately
Triggers: choosing a display format; presenter-led explanations; user-driven exploration
Method: 1. Use static views when the reading path is stable and self-contained. 2. Use animation when sequence or change must be revealed along a controlled path. 3. Use interaction when viewers need to inspect, filter, or compare according to their own questions.
Constraints: Interaction and motion must serve comprehension, not novelty.
Citation: cdv-select-static-animated-or-interactive | pages 82 | references/interactivity.md#cdv-select-static-animated-or-interactive

Capability: Test whether the audience perceives the intended insight
Triggers: validating a chart; testing comprehension; seeking design feedback
Method: 1. Ask a representative viewer to identify the key insight without coaching. 2. Use one specific comprehension question that can be answered from the visual. 3. Revise when the observed reading differs from the intended takeaway and retest.
Constraints: Do not treat general praise as evidence of comprehension.
Citation: cdv-test-with-audience | pages 139, 181 | references/storytelling.md#cdv-test-with-audience

Capability: Redesign a chart slide for clarity and ranking
Triggers: repairing a cluttered slide; showing rank order; improving chart legibility
Method: 1. Remove decorative backgrounds, 3D effects, unnecessary lines, and redundant marks. 2. Use readable type, formatted values, and the orientation that makes the intended ordering clear. 3. Place labels and legend where they minimize eye travel and verify the takeaway at presentation size.
Constraints: Preserve scale integrity and the data needed to support the comparison.
Citation: cdv-redesign-slide-for-clarity | pages 186, 187, 188, 189, 190, 191 | references/visual-design.md#cdv-redesign-slide-for-clarity

Capability: Use shared visuals to widen evidence-based decisions
Triggers: shared dashboards; broad organizational audiences; making analysis accessible
Method: 1. Identify which groups need access to the same evidence. 2. Provide a shared display that supports a common reading of the measures. 3. Pair access with definitions and context so availability becomes usable understanding.
Constraints: Shared access does not repair unclear measures or poor data quality.
Citation: cdv-share-data-for-decision-culture | pages 9 | references/data-visualization.md#cdv-share-data-for-decision-culture

Capability: Protect data when selecting visualization services
Triggers: using hosted visualization tools; working with sensitive data; evaluating free services
Method: 1. Determine how and where the service stores uploaded data. 2. Check whether a free tier makes data public or grants reuse rights. 3. Use an approved protected tier or a different tool when confidentiality requires it.
Constraints: Never upload sensitive data before storage and sharing terms are verified.
Citation: cdv-protect-data-in-visualization-tools | pages 51 | references/data-analysis.md#cdv-protect-data-in-visualization-tools

Capability: Build visualization skill through repeated applied practice
Triggers: improving visualization judgment; building team capability; turning guidance into routine
Method: 1. Integrate visual exploration and communication into the ordinary analytical workflow. 2. Practice on real data and compare outcomes against explicit criteria. 3. Record what improved audience understanding and reuse that learning.
Constraints: Tool fluency alone does not establish visualization competence.
Citation: cdv-build-a-visual-practice | pages 24, 25, 36, 262 | references/data-visualization.md#cdv-build-a-visual-practice

Capability: Ensure presentation readability and timing
Triggers: preparing slides; presenting charts live; reducing slide overload
Method: 1. Use type and chart labels that remain legible at the delivery distance. 2. Reduce text, table density, and annotation to what the audience can process in time. 3. Rehearse and record the presentation to verify pacing and completion.
Constraints: Treat room size, display conditions, and allotted time as design inputs.
Citation: cdv-ensure-presentation-readability | pages 182 | references/storytelling.md#cdv-ensure-presentation-readability

Capability: Remove non-data ink and emphasize the evidence
Triggers: decluttering a chart; improving a default chart; directing attention
Method: 1. Remove decorative backgrounds, borders, heavy grids, redundant ticks, and effects that add no meaning. 2. Use restrained axes, number formatting, and neutral support elements. 3. Add one justified emphasis mark for the comparison or statistic the audience should notice.
Constraints: Retain support elements needed for accurate reading and accessibility.
Citation: cdv-remove-non-data-ink | pages 125, 126, 127, 128, 129, 130 | references/visual-design.md#cdv-remove-non-data-ink

Capability: Frame the visual as evidence for a decision
Triggers: presenting findings; turning analysis into evidence; choosing what a chart must accomplish
Method: 1. Name the decision or understanding the visual must support. 2. Select only findings that materially support that purpose. 3. Make the evidence legible to the intended audience and state the takeaway.
Constraints: Do not let software choice substitute for an analytical purpose.; Do not imply causality or certainty beyond the underlying analysis.
Citation: cdv-visual-evidence-for-decisions | pages 9, 10, 54, 272 | references/data-visualization.md#cdv-visual-evidence-for-decisions

Capability: Apply a repeatable data-graphic design checklist
Triggers: refining a chart; standardizing visual quality; reviewing design details
Method: 1. Reduce chartjunk and keep non-data elements subordinate. 2. Check density, filtering, attribution, legibility, color, and alignment with the intended comparison. 3. Apply the checklist consistently and record deliberate exceptions.
Constraints: Aesthetic polish cannot compensate for inaccurate data or a mismatched chart form.
Citation: cdv-apply-design-standards | pages 137, 138 | references/visual-design.md#cdv-apply-design-standards

Capability: Understand and prepare data before encoding it
Triggers: starting a visualization; unfamiliar variables; reshaping data for charts
Method: 1. Read the data dictionary and establish what each variable and unit means. 2. Formulate visual questions from the supported attributes. 3. Rename and reshape fields into readable, analysis-ready structures before charting.
Constraints: Do not infer variable meaning from names alone.
Citation: cdv-understand-and-prepare-data | pages 90, 95, 97 | references/data-analysis.md#cdv-understand-and-prepare-data

Capability: Choose visualization tools by data scale and output needs
Triggers: selecting chart software; comparing static and interactive tools; working across data sizes
Method: 1. Inventory the data format, size, refresh pattern, and required destination. 2. Choose the smallest tool that supports the necessary chart form, interaction, and data scale. 3. Prototype the same view in candidate tools and compare effort, fidelity, and maintainability.
Constraints: Do not choose a tool solely from familiarity or novelty.
Citation: cdv-choose-tool-by-data-and-output | pages 42, 55 | references/data-visualization.md#cdv-choose-tool-by-data-and-output

Capability: Define visualization as a visual way to communicate data
Triggers: aligning a team on visualization; setting a visual brief; distinguishing decoration from communication
Method: 1. Describe the information or data to be communicated. 2. State the story, comparison, relationship, or pattern the audience must perceive. 3. Judge the graphic by whether it makes that meaning easier to understand.
Constraints: A graphic is not effective merely because it contains data.
Citation: cdv-define-visualization-purpose | pages 22 | references/storytelling.md#cdv-define-visualization-purpose

Capability: Design for clarity when interaction is unavailable
Triggers: reports; printed charts; non-interactive presentations
Method: 1. Make the intended reading path visible through hierarchy and chart structure. 2. Keep labels, encodings, and explanations sufficient for independent interpretation. 3. Remove cryptic detail and test the static view without presenter assistance.
Constraints: Do not rely on hover, filtering, or narration that the delivery medium cannot provide.
Citation: cdv-design-for-clarity-without-interaction | pages 159 | references/visual-design.md#cdv-design-for-clarity-without-interaction

Capability: Create deliberate opportunities for audience interaction
Triggers: live presentations; workshops; discussion-based data stories
Method: 1. Choose a point where a question or prediction will deepen understanding. 2. Invite a bounded response before revealing the relevant evidence. 3. Connect the response back to the chart and decision.
Constraints: Interaction must advance the evidence path rather than interrupt it.
Citation: cdv-invite-audience-interaction | pages 182 | references/interactivity.md#cdv-invite-audience-interaction
